overview.description: GOPS (short for 'Game of Pure Strategy'), also known as Goofspiel, is a celebrated card game in game theory and mathematics. It is a symmetrical contest where luck is almost entirely eliminated, as both players begin with identical sets of cards and are presented with the same sequence of 'prizes' to bid on. The game is a test of psychological reading and resource management, as players must decide which prizes are worth their highest 'bidding' cards and when to concede a small loss to save strength for a future win.

history.origins: GOPS was popularized by mathematicians and game theorists in the midnd20th century. Its earliest formal description appeared in the seminal 1957 textbook 'Games and Decisions' by Luce and Raiffa. It was designed to study zero-sum games with imperfect information.
timeline: 1940s: Variations played by soldiers in WWII using slips of paper.
1957: Formalized as Goofspiel in game theory literature.
1988: Influences the creation of the board game 'Hol's der Geier' (Raj).
Present: A standard example used in AI research to test sequence prediction and psychological modeling.
history.evolution: Has shifted from a math puzzle to a popular competitive card game often played by programmers and enthusiasts of the 'pure strategy' genre.
history.cultural: Regarded as the 'Chess of card games' because of its lack of a luckndheavy draw mechanic.

setup.deck:
A standard 52ndcard deck is divided into its four suits.
- Player 1: Takes all Clubs.
- Player 2: Takes all Spades.
- Prize Pile: The Diamonds are shuffled and placed face-down.
- (Hearts are removed from a 2ndplayer game).
setup.dealing: The basic game is for two players, using three suits from a standard 52-card pack.

rules.objective: Win the most points by capturing the highest-value prize cards (Diamonds).
rules.gameplay:
1. Reveal: The top card of the Diamond (Prize) pile is turned face-up.
2. Bid: Both players choose one card from their hand and place it face-down.
3. Showdown: Both bid cards are revealed simultaneously.
4. Award: The player with the higher bidding card wins the Diamond card and adds its value to their score.
5. Discard: Both bidding cards are discarded regardless of who won.
keyRules: Symmetry: Because both players have the same cards, the only difference is the order in which they play them.
No Re-use: Once you play your King, it is gone. If you waste your King on a 1ndpoint Ace, you have lost a massive strategic asset.
Winning condition: Win the most points by capturing the highest-value prize cards (Diamonds).

strategy.basic: Conserve your high cards for high prizes. Bidding a Jack for a 2 of Diamonds is almost always a mistake, as you leave yourself vulnerable when the King of Diamonds eventually appears.
strategy.intermediate: The 'N+1' Rule: Try to beat your opponent's likely bid by exactly one point. If you think they will play a 7 for an 8-prize, play an 8. Winning a trick by 1 point is the hallmark of efficient GOPS play.
strategy.advanced: Tie Manipulation: If a low-value prize is up (like a 3), and you suspect a tie will happen, you might deliberately play a very low card (like an Ace) to 'save' a midndtier card, knowing that you can fight for the rolledndover prize in the next round.
tips: Pay attention to what cards your opponent has already used. If they have already played their King and Queen, and you still have yours, you are in a dominant position for the final rounds.
If you cannot win a prize, play your lowest possible card (the 'trash card' strategy) to minimize your loss of bidding power.

difficulty.easy: Bids exactly the value of the prize card every time ('Naive Counter'); easy to beat by bidding prize+1.
difficulty.medium: Tracks opponent's remaining card set; uses basic N+1 logic; understands the value of tie roll-overs.
difficulty.hard: Uses psychological 'Mixed Strategy' (Nash Equilibrium); randomizes bids on certain prize values to avoid being read; calculates the 'Future Value' of a card based on the remaining prizes in the deck.

considerations: AI must avoid being predictable, as any pattern in GOPS can be immediately exploited.

engine.deckDescription: Standard 52-card deck comprising fifty-two cards: four suits of thirteen ranks each, with no jokers. Used for GOPS (Game of Pure Strategy) and variants.
engine.suitDescription: Four French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades), each with thirteen cards. Suits are used for auction and play in GOPS.
engine.rankDescription: Thirteen ranks per suit from Ace (high) through King, Queen, Jack, down to 2. Ranks determine trick and auction outcomes.
